item.title: When Your Only Tool Is An LLM-Hammer…
item.abstract: …you try and solve every problem with a prompt.When the term "AI" is used these days, it usually refers only to LLMs. Yet especially in the field of deep learning, there are many other exciting and important developments that you should be aware of if you want to integrate AI features into your software. In this session, we will establish initial guidelines to answer the following questions that are fundamental to project success:* When do I need an LLM? When do I need other models?* If I need an LLM: which one?* Where do I find such models and how do I choose the right one?* When do I need to train my own model, and when is an off-the-shelf solution sufficient?* What is the right way to integrate a model into my software?Knowing the answers to these questions will help you prevent many painful and expensive mistakes that most “AI” projects run into these days.

item.title: Your AI Demo Is Great. Your AI Bill Is Not.
item.abstract: Building Cost-Effective Systems in the Era of Expensive AI The era of “just throw an LLM at it” is ending. As AI companies raise prices, move toward IPOs, and optimize for profitability, teams are being forced to rethink how they build AI-powered products. Cost is no longer just an infrastructure concern; it is now a product, architecture, and business strategy problem. In this session, we’ll explore how to design AI systems that are useful, reliable, and cost-effective. We’ll look at where costs actually come from, including model calls, context size, retrieval, orchestration, evaluation, and unnecessary agentic complexity. We’ll discuss practical patterns for reducing spend: using smaller models where possible, caching, routing, prompt and context optimization, open-source models, hybrid architectures, and moving away from vendor lock-in. Attendees will leave with a framework for deciding when to use proprietary APIs, when to move to open-source models, and how to evaluate whether an AI feature is delivering real ROI.

item.title: Running Agents Locally with Open Source: From Laptop to Kubernetes
item.abstract: AI agents are everywhere, but most developers are building on top of proprietary APIs, paying per token, and hoping their sensitive data doesn't end up in someone else's training set. When things work, they work great. When you hit a rate limit, a price hike, or a data privacy wall, suddenly your production agentic application becomes a liability.The good news? The open source ecosystem has caught up with the release of open source models like Qwen 3.5. You can now run fully capable agentic AI systems, locally, on your own infrastructure, and at scale on Kubernetes, without compromising on model quality or developer experience.In this session, we'll build a working AI agent from scratch using an open source stack: Ollama for local inference, Podman to containerize the entire stack, and Model Context Protocol (MCP) to wire up tools your agent can actually use. Once it's working locally, we'll show the path to scaling it up onto OpenShift/Kubernetes, keeping the same architecture that worked on your laptop.You'll leave knowing how to:• Run open models locally with zero cloud dependency• Build an agent loop with real tools using MCP• Containerize your agent stack with Podman for reproducibility• Deploy and serve agents on Kubernetes with confidence

item.title: Embodied AI: Vision-Language Models Meet Physical Systems
item.abstract: Vision-language models are rapidly moving beyond digital tasks into systems that must perceive, decide, and act in the physical world. But this shift introduces an entirely different class of engineering challenges. In this talk, we explore hybrid architectures that combine the contextual reasoning of VLMs and VLAs with deterministic control loops, addressing the fundamental tension between the flexibility of neural inference and the hard timing guarantees required by physical actuators. We cover real-time visual perception on edge hardware, predictive models for latency-critical scenarios, and practical strategies for maintaining human-interpretable decision layers in autonomous systems. Drawing from use cases in active tracking, precision actuation, and autonomous navigation, we share where multimodal models genuinely add value over classical approaches — and where they don't.

item.title: Hybrid ML Systems: When to Use Rules, Small Models, and LLMs in Production
item.abstract: Rules, small models, or LLMs? In production, defaulting to "just use an LLM" is often the wrong call. Knowing when it's the right one is the actual skill.Using a production NLP pipeline that processes millions of receipts across diverse formats and languages, this talk gives a practical framework for hybrid ML architectures. We cover when rules still win on cost, latency, and auditability. We cover when a small, purpose-trained model is the right fit for high-volume extraction. And we cover when an LLM's flexibility justifies its cost, for example on long-tail layouts, ambiguous entity resolution, or adapting to new formats without retraining.We'll share concrete integration patterns: LLMs as fallback handlers, as rule and training-data generators, and as error evaluators. We'll also walk through the cost, latency, and reliability trade-offs each brings, and what broke when we got the boundaries wrong.You'll leave with a decision framework for combining rules, small models, and LLMs in production, instead of picking just one.

item.title: What gets measured gets optimized: evaluating the tools and skills your agents use
item.abstract: Everyone is shipping tools and skills for agents, but almost nobody can tell you whether theirs actually help. "It felt better in the demo" is not a metric, and with agents it is often wrong: something can look great in one transcript and quietly fail much of the time in aggregate. This deep dive shows how to put real numbers on the effectiveness and efficiency of agent-facing tools and skills. The order matters: effectiveness first, efficiency second, because saving cost is worthless if the agent never reaches the goal. Using real evaluation infrastructure as the worked example, I will cover how to run controlled with-and-without experiments scored against explicit checks, how to read the results to decide where to invest, an honest case where adding guidance made things worse, and the efficiency levers, and their trade-offs, that bring cost down once quality holds. You leave able to design an evaluation for your own agent tools instead of trusting a good-looking demo.

item.title: Building agent interfaces: designing for a user that is a machine
item.abstract: Increasingly the user of your software is not a human, it is an agent: one that decides in milliseconds, can be wrong, and that you cannot blindly trust. The common mistake is treating that agent as just a faster API client. It is not. It is its own kind of user, with its own strengths and bottlenecks, and agent experience is now part of your user experience. Drawing on real lessons from shipping tools that agents use every day, this talk walks through four engineering concerns that change when your user is a machine, each with a practical technique and an honest story of getting it wrong first: token usage and how to measure the real cost of a successful outcome, error recovery and self-healing, tool discoverability and why so many tool descriptions go unused, and trust boundaries, where the same capability needs a different security model depending on where it runs. The principles apply to any tool, API, or agent platform you build.

item.title: Spec Driven Development: The End of Vibe coding
item.abstract: Developers now create entire applications by simply chatting with AI tools. More and more startups rely on predominantly AI-generated code. But what initially thrilled developers quickly leads to frustration: generic code, poor architecture, and security vulnerabilities.In this talk, I demonstrate how Spec Driven Development (SDD) solves these problems. Instead of coding first and documenting later, SDD begins with precise specifications as the "single source of truth." Various tools and CLIs make this methodology practically applicable today with a structured 4-phase approach: Specify, Plan, Tasks, Implement.Using a real project, I show how SDD works with modern AI coding tools. I share honest insights from hands-on experience: where SDD excels, where it fails, and whether the specification overhead actually leads to better results.Attendees will learn when SDD makes sense, which tools are available, how to integrate this methodology into existing workflows, and why structured AI development could shape the future.Key takeaways: Practical SDD implementation, tool ecosystem overview, real-world examples, and critical evaluation of specification-driven AI development.

item.title: Teaching Machines to See and Read: The Science and Applications of Multimodal AI
item.abstract: Multimodality represents one of AI's most fascinating and business-actionable frontiers, yet its potential remains largely untapped. In this session, we'll explore multimodal architectures from CLIP to cutting-edge VLMs, discovering practical use cases where multimodal AI delivers real business value.

item.title: Designing Production-Ready Agentic Systems: Lessons from the Field
item.abstract: Building AI agents that work in the real world requires more than smart models—it requires hard trade-offs, strict constraints, a lot of context engineering and disciplined execution. In this talk, we share practical lessons learned from designing and deploying verticalized agents in production environments, including voice-based systems where latency and responsiveness are critical. We discuss why unconstrained autonomy often fails, how introducing deterministic budgets for reasoning and tool usage improves predictability and cost control, and how artifact-based memory patterns reduce data exposure while increasing traceability. Drawing from our experience with real-time voice models, we explore strategies for managing latency, parallel tool execution, and streaming interactions without sacrificing reliability. This session focuses on concrete deployment challenges, common failure modes, and actionable guidance for building agentic systems that move beyond demos and consistently perform under real-world constraints.

item.title: Model as Code: Code-Driven Model Development for Intelligent Apps with Small LLMs
item.abstract: AI-assisted development is transforming how we write software, but what if we applied the same software engineering rigor to the models themselves? In this talk, we introduce Model as Code: a practical, code-first approach to building intelligent applications where models become first-class, inspectable, testable, and composable citizens of the codebase. Instead of treating AI as opaque API black boxes, we define, configure, evaluate, version, and evolve models directly in code using familiar developer workflows, Git, CI/CD, and automated testing. We’ll explore how small language models and lightweight neural components can be deeply integrated into production applications when privacy, latency, cost, and on-device execution matter. Expect a hands-on, developer-centric journey: from describing model behavior in code, to connecting models with tools and context, safely evaluating changes, and iterating with confidence. The goal is to turn AI development from prompt magic into reliable engineering. Attendees will leave with a clear mental model and immediately applicable patterns for building AI-native applications where code, models, and agents evolve together.

item.title: Video Killed the Radio Star - UI is Dead, Long Live the Prompt Box
item.abstract:
The UI is dying. Within a few years — maybe months — the primary interface to most software will be a prompt box. When that happens, the application stack you've spent a decade building becomes invisible plumbing, and the agent calling it becomes the user.
That shift breaks almost every assumption baked into modern backends: REST endpoints designed for screens, auth flows that assume a human clicks "Allow," errors written for developers to debug, business logic scattered across UI state machines. Your services aren't ready to be talked to.
This talk shows how to retrofit an agentic layer onto existing backend services so they're ready when the UI disappears — drawn from a production system serving real traffic today. You'll leave with a concrete architecture, the patterns that worked, the ones that didn't, and a migration path that doesn't require throwing away what you already have.

item.title: Fine-Tuning Is the Easy Part: Adapting Open LLMs for Your Domain
item.abstract: Everyone asks which LoRA rank to use. Almost nobody checks what their run actually optimizes, and a fine-tune can finish cleanly while optimizing the wrong thing.Fine-tuning open LLMs is deceptively easy: the parts that look hard, the LoRA math and the training loop, are well understood and thoroughly tooled. You follow the tutorial, the loss goes down, the run finishes without a single error, and the model still comes out wrong. Or the run never starts, and the out-of-memory error won't tell you why. What decides whether a fine-tune works is the machinery around the training step: how your conversations become tokens and which of them carry the loss, where your GPU memory actually goes, and whether your evaluation can be trusted.This is a practitioner's tour of that machinery: when fine-tuning is the right lever and when prompting or retrieval serves you better; how chat templates and assistant-only loss masking really work, and how they break without an error message; LoRA and QLoRA demystified from first principles with the numbers that matter; why parameter-efficient fine-tuning still runs out of memory when the weight arithmetic says it shouldn't; and why your evaluation harness is harder to build than the fine-tune itself.You'll leave knowing which knobs matter, which are folklore, and which quick, preventative checks catch silent failures before they cost you a training run.

item.title: Build a private cluster for the office
item.abstract: For almost three years now John has been building private (local, shared server, private data room and private cloud) systems for his customers, mostly financial institutions, large banks, but also legal, medical and government work. Most of these organisations simply can't use the frontier models, even if hosted in the EU. It's not just cost, it's the need for long-term support, SLAs, total privacy, ownership, accountability, governance, repeatability, the list goes on... There's Bedrock and Vertex from Amazon and Google, and companies like RunPod with EU instances, but renting 24/7 costs roughly half the hardware's purchase price every month.For an office of about 10–50 people, not coders, a small redundant cluster of Mac Minis or Studios, NVIDIA DGX Sparks or even both are perfect for the job, dedicated or shared. John will start with setting up the machines, what needs networking and what doesn't, which models work best, adding tools and access to local data feeds, even private ones. He'll also cover KV-cache loading from SSD for near-instant document access to replace RAG. These models can code but that's not the main goal here, it's for private internal and customer data.This will be a technical talk but you will walk away with enough knowledge to start replacing your team's dependence on OpenAI, Anthropic and other frontier models. Open-weight models all the way.

item.title: From Lab to Production: Making Computer Vision Systems Work in the Real World
item.abstract: Most Computer Vision projects don't fail because of poor code; they fail when they enter production. In the lab, 99% accuracy is a triumph. Inproduction, that same model can become an undeployable liability due to data drift, concept drift, 5G connectivity gaps, or even simply overheating hardware.In this session, we move past the MLOps hype to explore a 5-step framework designed for B2B developers to bridge the gap between a "golden dataset" and a stable production architecture. We will walk through the critical decision matrix of task selection, map model architectures to hardware constraints (from NVIDIA Jetson toCloud-native), and discuss why the "Art" of AI lies in the long-term operations lifecycle. Attendees will leave with a practical checklist to ensure their next CV project ripens like fine wine rather than turning into "Day 2" technical debt.

item.title: Beyond Commercial Monoliths: How to Build a Vendor-Agnostic Invoice Extraction Pipeline with S(V)LMs and Visual Judging
item.abstract: Relying entirely on monolithic commercial Vision APIs for document processing introduces significant enterprise risks, including unpredictable costs, model deprecations, and silent updates. This presentation delivers a hands-on architectural analysis of a resilient alternative for scanned multi-page commercial invoices. We demonstrate how self-hosted, open-weights Small (Vision) Language Models (S(V)LMs) can be leveraged as a sovereign foundation for layout-aware, template-independent field extraction. To mitigate failures caused by document complexity—such as fragmented tables—we introduce a decoupled validation layer: self-hosted S(V)LMs perform the heavy lifting of data extraction, while Gemini 3.0 Flash is integrated strictly as a final visual judge. Auditing structured output against the original image eliminates vendor lock-in. Attendees will leave with a practical blueprint for building production-grade pipelines that ensure measurable extraction quality while maintaining architectural control and long-term cost stability.

item.title: The Failure-to-Metric Method: Building Evals Your Platform Can't
item.abstract: Building a custom eval metric is easy now; every platform lets you do it. The harder part, and the one that actually matters, is knowing which metric will serve your real business KPI.I call this the Failure-to-Metric method. Start from a real production failure, not a benchmark. Decide if it's even worth a dedicated metric. If it is, design it around the moment things went wrong, not just where they ended up: did the system refuse when it should have, and how costly was the answer when it didn't.I'll walk through how to recognize which failures actually matter and connect them to the KPI they're quietly damaging, using examples from high-stakes clinical workflows, where a wrong answer isn't just a bad user experience, it's a patient safety issue.Then I'll show two metrics built this way. A Refusal Rate metric, scoring whether the system correctly declines to answer when it should (higher is better). A Hallucination Specificity Score, scoring how dangerous the answer was when it didn't refuse (lower is better).You'll leave with the method, two working examples, and a way to decide which of your own production failures deserve a metric.

item.title: Context Engineering Is the New Prompt Engineering: Practical Patterns for Reliable Enterprise AI Agents
item.speakers: Sinda Khenine (Electrolux Rothenburg GmbH Factory and Development)
item.abstract: This session is the first part of a two-session journey from reliable enterprise AI agents to safely autonomous systems. It focuses on everything that enters the model’s context window.Carefully optimized prompts cannot prevent agents from using stale data, crossing permission boundaries, or producing decisions that cannot be reconstructed. Prompts shape how a model reasons, but context determines what it reasons about.The session presents practical patterns for selecting, securing, refreshing, validating, and observing context. It covers retrieval, token budgets, access control, data freshness, memory, provenance, validation, observability, and evaluation. Applying data engineering principles such as contracts, lineage, freshness guarantees, and testing makes agent failures measurable and diagnosable.This reliable context layer becomes the foundation for the second session, “From Answering to Acting,” which explores what must be engineered before an agent can safely execute actions.

item.title: Agents don’t need more tools. They need architecture.
item.abstract: Many agent prototypes start the same way: a model, a large prompt, lots of tools, and the hope that this will somehow become a product. At the latest, when tasks run for longer, users intervene, tools become risky, or multiple specialists are expected to collaborate, this pattern is no longer sufficient. This session is about how to think about agent systems architecturally. We will discuss multi-agent patterns, supervisor agents, agent networks, tool boundaries, memory, handoffs, observability, and human-in-the-loop UX. Using Mastra as an example of agent orchestration and AG-UI as an example of user-agent interaction, we will show how individual agents can be turned into robust, traceable workflows. The central question is: Where does collaboration between agents genuinely help, and where are we merely building a slow, expensive prompt conference? Participants will learn how to design, test, and debug agent systems without losing control of the system.

item.title: Beyond Single-Agent: Designing Multi-Agent Systems Around Failure Modes
item.abstract: Most multi-agent systems fail because they parallelize work without understanding how individual agents fail. This session turns modern benchmark error taxonomies—execution, coherence, and verification—into an architectural lens. We present a conceptual architecture where roles are matched to failure profiles: Planners maintain intent, Scouts gather information, Specialized Workers act, and Independent Verifiers challenge assumptions. Attendees will leave with a design checklist for building resilient agent stacks that allow coordination to genuinely outperform raw model capability, backed by insights from SOTA results on ARC-AGI-2 and Deep Research Bench.

item.title: Voice Agents - Where Latency Hides and How to Fight It
item.abstract: A voice agent pipeline looks simple: speech-to-text, LLM, text-to-speech. In practice, most of the engineering effort goes into things that aren't on that diagram. This talk breaks down the latency budget of a real-time voice agent and what has to happen between the user going silent and the agent starting to speak. I'll cover the parts that took us the longest to get right: detecting when someone actually stopped talking (harder than it sounds), streaming orchestration when components in your pipeline run at different speeds, handling interruptions without losing conversation context, and transport layer choices that affect how responsive the whole thing feels. I'll go through specific patterns we landed on as well as what didn't work and architectural choices we had to adapt. We'll also evaluate the newer speech-to-speech models and analyze their pros and cons for production deployments. If you're a developer who might end up building anything voice-based in the next time, this is the context you'll wish you had going in.

item.title: From Answering to Acting: Engineering Reliable Autonomous Enterprise Agents
item.speakers: Sinda Khenine (Electrolux Rothenburg GmbH Factory and Development)
item.abstract: This session is the second part of the journey and begins where “Context Engineering Is the New Prompt Engineering” ends. Once an agent’s context is selected, secured, fresh, attributable, and validated, the next question is whether it can safely be allowed to act.The session examines the controls required when agents move from generating answers to executing actions. It covers bounded reasoning loops, explicit state, budgets for steps, tokens, time, and cost, as well as tool contracts, action-time authorization, reversibility, approval gates, failure containment, and trajectory-level evaluation.The concepts from the first session continue on the action side: context budgets become action budgets, retrieval contracts become tool contracts, access permissions become authorization to act, and context provenance becomes a complete audit trail.Together, both sessions provide an end-to-end architecture for engineering reliable, observable, and gradually autonomous enterprise agents.

item.title: Designing Effective Synthetic Decision Personas
item.abstract: Adding more agents can make an AI system more capable, but it can also increase latency, cost, coordination overhead, and the number of ways the system can fail. The difficult engineering question is not how to connect multiple agents, but when they genuinely improve the result and how to organize their work effectively.This talk explores that question through the development of Synthetic Decision Personas: AI agents designed to represent distinct roles and perspectives in complex enterprise decisions. A central part of the work is comparing simpler, moderately complex, and more advanced architectures, then evaluating whether each additional layer produces enough improvement in quality and reliability to justify its cost.The second challenge is constructing the personas themselves. Reliable personas cannot come from role labels and prompts alone. The session will discuss how to validate that personas remain grounded in their evidence, behave consistently with their mandate, contribute genuinely different judgment, and improve as new decisions and outcomes become available.Attendees will gain a practical approach to building agentic systems and Synthetic Decision Personas that are reliable, accurate, efficient, and cost-conscious, from selecting the right architecture to constructing, validating, and improving the personas that operate within it.

item.title: Re-Imagine Anomaly Detection with GenAI
item.abstract: Gen AI is a game changer applied to many industries and businesses. How can we leverage Generative AI for anomaly detection? And what benefit can we extract by using GenAI in our setup?In this session I will address these issues. I will introduce you to a whole powerful family of Models you might not have heard from. It might even surprise you to hear, all the big players are involved in this research, Google, Meta, Facebook, and more. It is a frontier too few people have heard of, yet it might give you the edge you were looking for.Let me show you how you can use these models so you can implement anomaly detection in your company today!

item.title: Your Enterprise RAG Has No Legal Basis
item.abstract: Your RAG system works beautifully. Under GDPR, it has no legal basis to exist. Clean architecture. Proper embeddings. Maybe even agentic tool calling. You followed best practices. But when the auditor asks “what’s the legal basis for this processing?” there’s no answer. General-purpose “ask anything” chatbots have no defined purpose. Without a defined purpose, no legal basis can exist under GDPR. The architecture itself is the violation. In this talk, we’ll live-code a “best practices” enterprise knowledge bot, then ask the questions nobody asks: Where is purpose limitation enforced? Where is legal basis documented? I’ll show why anonymization doesn’t save you. 97% accuracy isn’t “anonymous” under GDPR. It’s still PII. Then I’ll show you the fix: a purpose-scoped bot architecture where legal basis is a first-class configuration item. Each bot gets a defined purpose, scoped data access, configured tools, and documented legal basis. The architecture enforces the boundaries. The retrieval layer can only access documents within that bot’s scope. Non-compliance becomes architecturally impossible. The good news? You didn’t waste your investment. This is a 50k governance layer, not a rewrite.

item.title: From Demos to Durable Agents: Engineering the Reliability Stack for Production
item.abstract:
Everyone can build an AI agent demo in a weekend, but shipping one that works reliably in a 24/7 high-stakes environment—like institutional finance or crypto market intelligence—is a massive engineering challenge. This session moves past the "vibe coding" hype to dive into the hard-technical "Reliability Stack" required to turn fragile LLM scripts into durable, production-ready systems.
Drawing from firsthand experience building research and trading agents at a leading blockchain analytics firm (Nansen), I will detail the architectural patterns used to solve the "Agentic Loop" problem. Key topics include:
State-Machine Orchestration: Moving from simple RAG to structured state machines to prevent reasoning loops.
Non-Deterministic Evaluation: Implementing "LLM-as-a-Judge" frameworks and semantic unit testing to quantify performance.
The Reliability Stack: Deploying guardrails, circuit breakers, and "Reasoning Trace" observability to debug autonomous failures in real-time.
Governance in Finance: Building audit trails and decision boundaries that satisfy both users and compliance.
Attendees will leave with a practical framework for evaluating agent readiness and a checklist of failure modes that only appear at scale.

item.title: Run LLMs Locally
item.abstract:
LLMs are increasingly accessible, yet their deployment typically relies on cloud services that raise privacy, security and cost concerns for researchers, developers and end‑users. This talk will present a fully reproducible pipeline for running state‑of‑the‑art LLMs locally on commodity laptops equipped with integrated AMD GPUs and Ubuntu. The live demo will demonstrate how to run models like Qwen, Gemma and Mellum locally with competitive latency and memory usage on a single machine with 32 GB RAM and an AMD Ryzen 7 cpu.
Key contributions of the talk include:
1. Hardware‑software co‑design: detailed requirements (kernel version, GTT configuration, driver flags) and a step‑by‑step guide to enable direct GPU memory access via RADV and the Linux kernel.
2. Inference workflow: end‑to‑end instructions for downloading pre‑quantized GGUF models, launching llama‑server, and interacting through a web UI or OpenAI‑compatible API endpoints.
3. Performance evaluation: Demo with benchmark results (latency, throughput, memory footprint), illustrating the trade‑offs between model size, precision, and GTT memory.
4. Security: Prompt Injection example, prevention strategies
Audience members will leave with a ready‑to‑run setup, scripts, and understanding of how to harness their own hardware for secure, cost‑effective LLM inference. (Disclaimer: this abstract was generated locally with GPT-OSS 20B, running at 18.9 tokens/sec).

item.title: Avoid data leakage in Agentic RAG by using ReBAC
item.abstract:
We’ve recently seen the rise of Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) systems. With the proliferation of AI Agents & LLMs in Enterprise, the next step in the evolution is Agentic RAG. But this introduces a subtle but critical problem: authorization is no longer a single check, but a chain of decisions across tools, memory, and retrieval layers and this breaks more often than you expect.
This talk is a deep dive into how modern authorization systems can ensure that AI Applications have access only to authorized data. The talk will look at why the Google Zanzibar model of authorization which uses Relationship-Based Access Control (ReBAC) is well suited to handle dynamic, relationship-driven authorization at scale. The talk explains how the Google Zanzibar system works under the hood, and how to apply it to Agentic RAG with techniques such as pre-filteration and post-filteration. Learning these fundamentals might just prevent broken access control issues in your application.
The talk will also include a live coding demo implementing authorization for Agentic RAG using Open Source tools such as Weaviate, Langchain, and SpiceDB.
